title: How Scientists Lived Frozen Into the Arctic Ice for a Whole Year
asof: Figures from the MOSAiC expedition 2019–2020 · sources in description

shots.s: In 2019, a ship sailed into the Arctic
and let the ice freeze around it.
On purpose.
For a year, it drifted with the ice,
past the North Pole.
For months, the sun never rose.
It got down to minus forty-two degrees.
And polar bears came to visit.
So how do you eat,
sleep,
and work,
frozen into the ice?
This is Polarstern,
a German research icebreaker.
The mission was called MOSAiC.
The biggest Arctic research expedition ever.
The idea was over a hundred years old.
In the 1890s, the explorer Fridtjof Nansen froze his ship Fram into the ice on purpose.
MOSAiC did the same,
with modern labs.
The ship found a floe about two
and a half by three and a half kilometers.
Then it let the ice close in around it.
The ship was home for everyone.
It carries cooks, a baker,
a doctor, and even a post office.
All the labs, workshops and offices are on board.
Polarstern has space for up to forty-four crew
and fifty-five scientists.
Over the year,
three hundred and thirty-seven scientists and experts took part.
They came in shifts of about two months.
From thirty-seven nationalities.
In their downtime,
people exercise or hang out in the lounges.
Next to the ship, they built a town on the ice.
They called it the Ice Camp.
Neighborhoods for each science team.
One was called ROV City,
for the underwater robots.
One was called Ocean City.
Five kilometers of power cable,
laid across the ice.
Lights can disturb the ice ecosystem.
So part of the camp was a dark zone,
with infrared light only.
Out here, you're not at the top of the food chain.
A big male polar bear can weigh around six hundred kilos.
So nobody walks onto the ice without a bear guard.
Six to eight guards on each leg of the trip.
They watch the horizon from the ship,
or patrol a tripwire fence around the camp.
If a bear crosses the wire,
a flare goes off to scare it away.
More than sixty polar bears were spotted near the ship.
Not a single one was shot.
In winter, the sun didn't rise for about a hundred
and fifty days.
Only the moon and stars light the ice.
The coldest reading was minus forty-two point three.
With the wind, it felt like minus sixty-five.
The ice moves.
Cracks open up right through the camp.
And the ship is up
to fifteen hundred kilometers from the nearest town.
You can't drive to the store.
So other icebreakers break through to resupply you.
In early 2020,
the Russian icebreaker Kapitan Dranitsyn arrived.
It brought new people
and forty-three tons of supplies.
The ice was so thick that it ran low on fuel itself.
Another icebreaker had to come to refuel it.
Then, in spring, COVID hit.
Borders closed.
Planned crew-swap flights were called off.
Polarstern left the floe for a few weeks
to meet two other German research ships.
Then it went back to the ice.
Then the sun came back.
And in summer, it never set.
The ice started melting.
Pools of water formed on top.
After three hundred days,
the first floe broke apart.
The team found a second floe near the North Pole.
They worked there for another thirty days.
In October 2020,
Polarstern returned to Germany.
It had drifted three thousand four hundred kilometers.
It got within a hundred
and fifty-six kilometers of the North Pole.
Over a thousand ice cores came home with it.
And more than a thousand weather balloons had been launched.
Could you live a year frozen into the ice?
